Module 3 is where you stop describing prompts and start running them. Three periods, two hands-on activities and one dataset. Everything you need is attached to this lesson.

## What is attached

- **Lecture notes (PDF).** The notes for the whole course. Module 3 is Periods 7 to 9, sections 7.1 to 9.5. Use them for the full wording, the verified tables and the practice questions at the end of each period.
- **Slides, 150 pages (PDF).** The complete deck with checkpoint questions and key takeaways.
- **Slides, 81 pages (PDF).** The short version, for a quick preview or revision.
- **Activity 1 sheet, Student version (PDF).** *AI-Assisted Retail Data Visualisation*, Case 1, Period 7. About 55 to 70 minutes of practice.
- **Activity 2 sheet, Student version (PDF).** *Human vs AI-Assisted Prompt Design (A/B/C)*, Period 8. About 70 to 90 minutes of practice.
- **The CSV.** `Slidescope_Retail_Store_Sales_Enhanced_2025.csv`, used by both activities.

The activity times are practice time on top of the 45-minute lessons; they do not change the course schedule. Activity 3 belongs to Module 4 and is attached there.

## Where each period is

| Period | Lecture notes | Slides (150 pages) | Slides (81 pages) | Activity |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 7 Task Execution, Data Visualisation Case | 7.1 to 7.6 | 68 to 78 (checkpoint on 77) | 39 to 45 | Activity 1 |

The Module 3 opener is slide 67 of the long deck. The short deck covers only the opening slide of Period 9.

## The CSV in one minute

200 transactions, 13 columns, one row per transaction: `Transaction_ID`, `Store_Region`, `Product_Category`, `Payment_Method`, `Customer_Type`, `Unit_Price`, `Items_Sold`, `Gross_Amount`, `Discount_Percent`, `Discount_Amount`, `Net_Sales_Amount`, `Average_Price_Per_Item`, `Effective_Discount_Per_Item`.

- Four regions: East, North, South, West. Four product categories: Apparel, Electronics, Furniture, Grocery.
- The file has **no dates, no costs or profit and no currency**, and no customer identities. Everything you conclude must stay inside that.
- In the spreadsheet, region is column B and `Net_Sales_Amount` is column K.

> [!canh-bao] Use an institutionally approved chatbot and upload only this teaching CSV. Do not add private or confidential business records.

## How to use them

1. **Before a period:** skim the matching slides to see the shape of the task.
2. **In the lesson:** try each "Predict" and "Find the error" box before opening it, then do the quiz and rate your confidence for every question.
3. **After the quiz:** read the matching sections of the lecture notes.
4. **Activities:** work in a spreadsheet next to the chatbot. Keep an untouched copy of the CSV and build your own pivot table. Figures in the lessons were recalculated from the file, but a chatbot's answer will vary from run to run, so always check the tool's numbers against yours.
5. **For revision:** use the flashcards at the end of each lesson, then return to the short slides.

> [!meo] Each activity has an Assignments tab in its lesson (Activity 1 in Period 7, Activity 2 in Period 8). The Student sheet is the full instruction; the assignment tab is where you submit.

lessons.body:
A regional manager sends you one line: *"Which of our four regions sells the most? I need a chart for tomorrow."* You have the 200-row retail CSV and a chatbot that can draw a bar chart in seconds. The chart will look professional whatever it contains. This period is about the work between "the chatbot answered" and "I can put this in front of the manager". You will run the full cycle, **Define → Design → Execute → Evaluate → Refine**, on one small task, Case 1.

> [!ghi-nho] Case 1 is the whole course in miniature. A fluent, good-looking answer is only a draft. It becomes evidence after you have checked the numbers, the scale and every sentence of interpretation against the CSV.

:::Predict before you read
Before you look at any table in this lesson, write down two guesses: (1) which region has the **highest total** net sales, and (2) which region has the **highest average net sales per transaction**. Are they the same region? You will check both guesses in section 7.3.
:::

## The five-step cycle on Case 1

| Stage | What you do in Case 1 |
|---|---|
| **Define** | Fix the question, the audience, the deliverables and what the chart cannot say |
| **Design** | Write the chart prompt: grouping field, measure, aggregation rule, scale, labels, exclusions |
| **Execute** | Run it in a tool that can really read the file and draw charts (or use the honest fallback) and save the actual output |
| **Evaluate** | Check the measure, all four totals, the axis, the labels and every written claim against the CSV |
| **Refine** | Make one visible improvement, rerun, then recheck |

The question is **descriptive**: "Which region has the highest and which the lowest total net sales in the provided file?" A bar chart of four named categories can answer that. It cannot show whether a region is improving (the file has no dates), whether it is profitable (no costs) or whether it runs more efficiently (no store counts or opening hours).

## Define: question, output and data

Define the manager's question as a regional net-sales comparison, then ask for four deliverables: a **chart**, a **four-row table**, a **short interpretation** (two or three sentences) and **one documented source check**.

The input is the complete 200-row CSV. The grouping field is `Store_Region`, the measure is `Net_Sales_Amount` and the aggregation is **SUM**. If the question is "how much in total?", do not average individual sales. Count transactions (`Transaction_ID`) as well if the manager needs to tell *total recorded value* from *how often sales happen*.

> [!canh-bao] "Net sales" is not "gross sales" and not "profit". The file also has Gross_Amount, Discount_Amount and Unit_Price. Name the exact column in the prompt, or the tool may choose a different one.

## Design: write the chart prompt

Compare two prompts for the same task.

```prompt Prompt A — vague
Make a sales chart by region for my manager.
```

*Why it is weak:* it does not say which column is the measure, whether to sum or average, whether the axis starts at zero, what to do about currency or what not to claim. The chatbot fills every gap with a guess, and you will not know which guesses it made.

```prompt Prompt B — verifiable
Using the attached retail CSV, calculate SUM(Net_Sales_Amount) and COUNT(Transaction_ID) for each Store_Region. Show the table and a horizontal bar chart sorted by net sales, with the axis starting at zero. Label the axis "Total net sales (currency unspecified)". Show the overall total as a check and explain the grouping method in two sentences. Do not add dates, profit, targets or causal explanations.
```

*Why it is better:* every field is named, the aggregation is explicit, the scale is fixed, a check total is requested and unsupported content is excluded. Each sentence changes something you can test afterwards. It is not better because it is longer: "make it look professional" would add words but nothing checkable.

Here is the reference table, calculated from the full CSV. Compare it with your two guesses.

| Region | Transactions | Total net sales | Net sales per transaction |
|---|---|---|---|
| North | 57 | 260,026.33 | 4,561.87 |
| South | 53 | 236,980.99 | 4,471.34 |
| West | 51 | 213,240.41 | 4,181.18 |
| East | 39 | 182,004.38 | 4,666.78 |
| **Total** | **200** | **892,252.11** | **4,461.26** |

North has the highest total and East the lowest. But East has the **highest** net sales per transaction, because it has far fewer transactions (39). A region with the smallest total is not automatically the weakest, which is one more reason not to write "best" or "worst" under a chart of sums.

The overall 4,461.26 is 892,252.11 / 200. It is **not** the average of the four regional averages (that would give about 4,470.29). The transaction counts must add up to 200 and the four totals to 892,252.11; if either fails, something was dropped or double-counted.

> [!meo] Keep full precision in calculations and round only for display. If chart labels are rounded (for example to thousands), say on the chart that the rounding is for display only.

## Execute: run the prompt and keep the evidence

Run the prompt in a chatbot with genuine file-analysis and chart capability, where you have one. Start by asking it to report the **row count and column names** it sees. If it says 200 rows and 13 columns, you have some evidence that it read the file rather than guessed.

If the tool cannot open the CSV or draw a chart, use an honest fallback:

1. Build a pivot table in a spreadsheet (rows `Store_Region`, values SUM of `Net_Sales_Amount`) and draw the chart there. Label it "spreadsheet-created".
2. Or paste your four checked totals into the chatbot, say where they came from and ask for a chart specification or a caption.
3. Never write that the chatbot analysed a file or drew a chart when it did not.

Save the prompt version, the tool and model (if visible), the run date and the actual response and chart. Leave the original CSV unchanged.

> [!canh-bao] A chart that appears on screen proves nothing about how it was made. Some tools describe a chart they never drew, or draw one from numbers they invented. Your own pivot table is what turns the output into evidence.

sections.title: 7.5 Evaluate: check the chart and its claims
sections.intro: A correct ranking does not prove why regions differ. Before you accept an AI chart, run these five checks.

parts.title: Measure
parts.md: Is it **net sales**, not gross sales, discounts or profit? The axis title and the chart title must say so. "Most profitable region" is a wrong title for this chart; "Recorded net sales by store region" is a suitable one.

parts.title: Values
parts.md: Recalculate each regional sum from the CSV. The four counts must add up to 200 and the four totals to the whole-file sum.

parts.title: Scale
parts.md: Bars encode value by **length**, so the axis must start at zero. A truncated axis makes a modest gap look enormous.

parts.title: Labels and units
parts.md: All four region names are present and correct. The file gives no currency, so none may appear. If values are rounded, the chart says it is for display only.

parts.title: Claims
parts.md: For each sentence ask: which number in my table supports this? "North has the highest recorded net sales" passes. "North's stores are more efficient" and "East is declining" have no support in the file.

sections.outro:
Practise on a deliberately flawed answer. The text below is **invented for practice; it is not the output of a real run**.

:::Find the error
> **Chart title:** Most profitable region
>
> The vertical axis starts at 150,000. The labels read "$260,026", "$236,981" and "$213,240". The three bars are North, South and West.
>
> **Commentary:** "North leads. East is missing because its sales declined and caused a loss."

Write down every problem you can find. There are at least five.
:::

:::Open the solution after you have tried
1. The title says *profit*; the chart shows net sales.
2. The axis starts at 150,000, not zero, so bar lengths exaggerate the gaps.
3. The dollar signs add a currency the file never states.
4. East is missing, so the four-region comparison is incomplete.
5. "Declined" needs dates and "caused a loss" needs costs and causes. The file has none of these, so the sentence must be deleted.

Notice that the numbers themselves might be right. A chart can be **correct and still misleading**, and its commentary can be unsupported even when the chart is sound. Judge them separately.
:::

> [!ghi-nho] Fix what is wrong, keep what is verified. One bad sentence is no reason to throw away four correct totals, and four correct totals are no reason to publish one bad sentence.

sections.title: 7.6 Refine: improve the chart without changing the evidence

parts.md:
Refinement should answer a **visible problem**: hard-to-read order, clutter, labels that do not help the manager find the answer in 20 seconds. It never changes the underlying numbers.

```prompt Refinement follow-up
Keep the verified regional sums unchanged. Sort the bars from highest to lowest, remove distracting gridlines, highlight North and East, and use rounded labels in thousands. Keep the zero baseline. Add a short footnote: the file has no dates, costs or currency. Do not make causal claims.
```

*Why it works:* it says what must stay fixed (sums, zero baseline) before it says what to change, and it asks for a footnote that keeps the limits visible. Compare it with "make it look better", which invites the tool to change anything.

| May change | Must not change |
|---|---|
| Order of bars, colours, gridlines, label size, rounding for display | The four totals, the measure, the zero baseline, the four region labels |
| Wording of title and footnote, if it becomes more accurate | A claim that the data do not support |

After the rerun, compare both versions and **recheck** all four values, the axis labels and the meaning of the bars. A reversed order with correct totals usually means the sort criterion changed; check that first. Save both outputs and write one sentence on why the revised chart is easier to read.

1. Open the CSV in a spreadsheet and keep an untouched copy of the original sheet.
2. Insert a pivot table with `Store_Region` in rows and SUM of `Net_Sales_Amount` in values. Alternatively use a formula such as `=SUMIF(Raw!B2:B201, A2, Raw!K2:K201)` after naming the sheet *Raw*. Region is column B and net sales column K.
3. Compare each of the four sums with the chart or table the AI gave you. Add the four sums and compare with SUM of all 200 values in column K.
4. Look at the first tick on the value axis and at every label and unit.
5. Read each interpretation sentence and find the number that supports it.

**Keep a verification record** with the task brief, the original prompt, the input filename and version, the verified table, the first chart, the checks you made, the revised prompt and the final chart. Add two or three sentences about what improved and **one claim you deliberately avoided**. A classmate should be able to recreate the four totals from your record without copying the AI output.

> [!vi-du] A caption that passes: "North has the largest total recorded net sales in this file and East the smallest. These are sums of recorded transactions; they are not adjusted for transaction counts or store numbers and say nothing about profit or causes."

**Try it:** (1) explain why a line chart suits four unordered region names badly; (2) name two design changes that improve a correct bar chart without changing its values; (3) write a one-sentence caption with one verified observation and one limit.

**Activity 1** applies this whole cycle to the CSV. Open the Assignments tab of this lesson for the task and rubric, and the Student activity sheet attached to the Module 3 materials lesson.

items.example: SUM(Net_Sales_Amount) grouped by Store_Region gives four numbers from 200 rows.

items.meaning: For "how much in total?" use SUM. An average of individual sales answers a different question (typical size of one sale).
items.example: East has the lowest total but the highest average per transaction.

items.meaning: A value axis that starts at zero. Bars encode value by length, so a truncated axis exaggerates differences.
How a chart maps data to visual features such as bar length and position. Check that the encoded measure is the one you asked for.

Measure, values, scale, labels and units, claims. A correct ranking never explains why regions differ.
A written description of a chart (data, type, axes, labels) that you can build in another tool. Use it when the chatbot cannot draw.
A pivot table or SUMIF formula that reproduces the grouped totals independently. State honestly which output came from the spreadsheet.
Improving readability (order, clutter, emphasis, labels) while keeping values, measure and baseline unchanged, then rechecking.

summary: Case 1 runs the full cycle on one chart: define the question, write a verifiable prompt, execute and save the real output, evaluate it against the CSV, then refine.
Establish correct aggregated numbers first: SUM of Net_Sales_Amount by Store_Region, four transaction counts that add up to 200, and an overall total that reconciles.
Judge the chart for the right measure, a zero baseline, complete labels, no invented units and claims that stay inside the data. Ranking is not explanation.
Refine one visible problem, keep the values fixed, recheck, and save both versions with the checks you made.

questions.prompt: During a chart task, which step comes immediately after Execute in the course cycle?
questions.explanation: In Define → Design → Execute → Evaluate → Refine, Evaluate comes straight after Execute: the tool has produced something and now you check it against the CSV. Publishing immediately skips that stage, and it is the tempting mistake because a finished-looking chart feels done. Redefining the objective belongs earlier in the cycle.

options.label: Rewrite all constraints automatically
Publish the chart immediately
Evaluate the produced result
Redefine the original objective

questions.prompt: What is the chart task in Case 1?
questions.explanation: The CSV has Store_Region and Net_Sales_Amount for 200 undated transactions, so the comparison it supports is total net sales by region. Profit margin needs costs, a monthly forecast needs dates and store visits are not recorded. Profit margin is the tempting wrong choice because it sounds like what a manager wants, but the file has no cost field.

options.label: Forecast monthly revenue by region
Compare profit margin by region
Compare total net sales by region
Estimate store visits by region

questions.prompt: A chart shows East as 182,004.38 and North as 260,026.33. Which interpretation is justified?
questions.explanation: Two sums establish a ranking of recorded net sales: North is higher than East. They cannot show margin, demand or efficiency, which need costs, customer data or store counts. "Demand" is the tempting choice because high sales feel like high demand, yet sales also depend on prices, store size and the number of transactions.

options.label: North's recorded net sales are higher
North's profit margin is higher
North's customer demand is higher
North's stores are more efficient

questions.prompt: A bar chart starts its vertical axis at 180,000 and magnifies small differences. What edit best supports fair reading?
questions.explanation: Bars encode value by length, so every bar must start from the same zero baseline. With an axis starting at 180,000, East's bar (182,004) would look about forty times shorter than North's, although East's total is about 70% of North's. Removing axis labels hides the distortion instead of fixing it.

options.label: Scale each bar independently by region
Remove labels from the vertical axis
Use a zero baseline for these bars
Replace amounts with decorative icons

questions.prompt: What should be checked when reviewing an AI-made regional chart?
questions.explanation: A chart is analytically sound when its labels name the right measure, its totals match the CSV and every stated claim is supported. Colours, fonts, animation and image size change how it looks, not whether it is right. Brand colours are the tempting choice because they are easy to see, which is exactly why they are not evidence.

options.label: Manager's mood and meeting venue
Image size and animation effects
Labels, totals and stated claims
Brand colors and font novelty

questions.prompt: Your chatbot cannot create a chart from the uploaded file. What is a workable fallback?
questions.explanation: If the chatbot cannot draw a chart, ask for a chart specification that you check and build with another permitted tool (or draw the chart in a spreadsheet from verified totals). A capability cannot be assumed without seeing it executed. Many tools do draw charts, which makes the first option tempting, but you must confirm what your tool actually did.

options.label: Claim every interface supports charts
Report imaginary plot coordinates
Assume an unseen chart was created
Request a checked chart specification

questions.prompt: The chart's order is reversed after a revision, but the totals stay correct. What should be done?
questions.explanation: When the order is reversed but the totals stay correct, the sort criterion has most likely changed (for example ascending instead of descending). Check that first, separately from totals and labels. Deleting the CSV or doubting the amounts are over-reactions, and reading the reversal as demand growth invents a cause.

options.label: Check whether the ranking criterion changed
Describe the reversal as demand growth
Delete the input CSV and restart
Assume the amounts also became wrong

questions.prompt: Two charts use the same verified totals; one has a truncated bar axis and one uses zero. Which is preferable for relative sizes?
questions.explanation: The totals are identical, so the difference is the scale. A shared zero baseline with clear units keeps bar lengths proportional to values. A truncated axis without a note distorts relative size, bars rescaled individually cannot be compared, and larger decorative labels do not repair either problem.

options.label: The zero-baseline chart with clear units
The truncated chart with no scale note
The chart with bars rescaled individually
The chart with larger decorative labels

questions.prompt: The AI chart labels values as dollars. What is the specific problem?
questions.explanation: The file never states a currency, so dollar labels add a unit that nothing in the data supports; the axis should say "currency unspecified". The other problems are invented: Net_Sales_Amount is numeric and can be summed, every row has a Transaction_ID and four categories are easy to read.

options.label: Currency was never specified in the file
The net-sales figures cannot be summed
The chart contains too many categories
The regional data lack transaction IDs

questions.prompt: The revised chart looks clearer but omits West. Which review finding is strongest?
questions.explanation: The manager asked for a four-region comparison, so leaving out West fails completeness however clean the chart looks. The omission does not prove that West has no sales, a tidier look does not make the numbers more precise, and nothing here measures store efficiency.

options.label: The chart now measures store efficiency
The omission proves West has no sales
The chart fails regional completeness
The chart improves numerical precision

questions.prompt: Which prompt best defines a verifiable regional chart?
questions.explanation: A verifiable prompt names the measure (net sales), the grouping (region) and a checkable requirement (every bar labelled), so you can recompute the result. "Striking", "deserves the most praise" and "most successful marketing effort" are subjective or need data the file lacks. The first of these sounds like a designer's brief, but nothing in it can be checked.

options.label: Sum net sales by region; label every bar
Make a striking sales graphic for leaders
Show which region deserves the most praise
Find the most successful marketing effort

questions.prompt: The AI returns a correct chart but argues East's decline caused a loss. What is the right disposition?
questions.explanation: A chart and its narrative can be judged separately. The totals check out, so keep the chart. No dates, causes or profit figures support "decline" or "loss", so remove that claim. Rejecting every total discards verified work, publishing both lets an unsupported claim ride on a correct chart, and a profit estimate would invent data.

options.label: Reject all totals because text is flawed
Retain the chart; remove the causal claim
Replace the claim with a profit estimate
Publish both because the chart is correct

questions.prompt: A student records the initial prompt and the revised chart prompt. What else improves comparison?
questions.explanation: Comparing versions requires both prompts, both outputs and the check results; together they make the work traceable and repeatable. Keeping only the final screenshot or deleting the CSV removes the evidence, and renaming the initial prompt as final falsifies the record.

options.label: Keep only the final screenshot
Rename the initial prompt as final
Delete the regional CSV after use
Save both outputs and the check results

questions.prompt: Put the steps of Case 1 in the order you would carry them out.
questions.explanation: You define the task first, write a prompt that names fields and checks, run it and save the real output, verify it independently against the CSV, and only then refine and recheck. Refining before verifying would polish a chart whose numbers you have not confirmed.
sequence: Write the task brief: question, audience, four deliverables
Write the chart prompt with named fields, SUM and a zero baseline
Run it and save the actual output with prompt version, tool and date
Recalculate the four totals in a spreadsheet and check labels, axis and claims
Write a follow-up for one design change, rerun and recheck

questions.prompt: East has 39 transactions and total net sales of 182,004.38. What is East's net sales per transaction, to two decimal places?
questions.explanation: 182,004.38 / 39 = 4,666.78. This is the highest figure among the four regions, even though East has the lowest total. A total and an average answer different questions, so check which one the manager asked for.

questions.prompt: Match each chart problem to the right fix.
questions.explanation: Each fix repairs the specific fault without changing the verified data: restore a zero baseline, name the real measure, remove an unsupported unit and put back the omitted region. None of the fixes involves altering the totals.

pairs.right: Retitle it "Recorded net sales by store region"
Remove the currency or state that it is unspecified
Restore all four regions and rerun the grouping

assignments.description:
## Activity 1 · AI-assisted retail data visualisation (Case 1)

**Period 7 · about 55 to 70 minutes of practice · CLO2, CLO3, CLO4.** Full Student sheet: attached to the Module 3 materials lesson.

### Business question and goal

A retail manager wants a comparison of the four store regions. **Question: which region contributes the most total net sales?** Deliver a four-region calculation table, a bar chart and a brief, evidence-based interpretation. Improve the chart after you have checked it.

**Success standard.** Use every transaction in the source CSV, the exact fields `Store_Region` and `Net_Sales_Amount`, a zero baseline on the bar chart and all four region labels. Do not invent a currency, a profit figure or an explanation for differences in sales.

### What you need

- `Slidescope_Retail_Store_Sales_Enhanced_2025.csv` (200 transactions, 13 columns).
- A spreadsheet (Excel, Google Sheets or equivalent) and, if available, an approved chatbot. No coding.
- Fallback: if your chatbot cannot open CSV files, calculate the totals in a spreadsheet and paste the four-row result into the chatbot with a provenance note. If it cannot draw a chart, draw it in the spreadsheet. State the real role of the chatbot; never claim it analysed a file or made a chart when it did not.

### Workflow

**Define (5 min).** Write a task brief: decision user (retail manager), question, output (four-row table, bar chart, 2 to 3 sentences of interpretation, check record) and success checks (all four regions, accurate sums, zero baseline, no unsupported claims).

**Design (10 min).** Open the CSV, locate `Transaction_ID`, `Store_Region` and `Net_Sales_Amount`, and check that there are four named regions and numeric net sales. Adapt the starter prompt in your own words and save it as **V1**.

```prompt Starter prompt V1
Use the attached retail CSV. Treat each row as a transaction. Group records by Store_Region and compute SUM(Net_Sales_Amount) for each of the four regions. Give a table with exact values to two decimals and show the aggregation method. Create a bar chart with region labels, a clearly named measure and a zero baseline. State that currency is unspecified. Give one finding supported by the table; do not claim profit, trends or causes.
```

**Execute (10 min).** Run V1 with the CSV (or disclose the spreadsheet-only fallback). Record the chatbot name or model, the date and whether it really read the data. Save the returned table and chart, or screenshots. If there is no chart support, make a bar chart from the verified spreadsheet table and label it "spreadsheet-created". Locate the exact calculation the tool claims; if it could not calculate it, record that limitation.

**Evaluate (15 min).** In a separate Summary worksheet, build a pivot table (rows `Store_Region`, values SUM of `Net_Sales_Amount`) or a SUMIF formula, without overwriting the source data. Record:

| Check | What you must record |
|---|---|
| Group totals | Four independent spreadsheet sums, each compared with V1 |
| Grand total | The four regional totals added together, compared with SUM of all raw `Net_Sales_Amount` |
| Encoding | Four correct region labels, bar height represents net sales, vertical axis starts at zero |
| Interpretation | Name the highest region using verified evidence; give no cause or currency claim |

**Human verification gate.** If any sum, label or scale is wrong, fix the calculation or the chart before you refine. A fluent AI response is not a substitute for a cross-check.

**Refine (10 min).** Choose **one** improvement: sort the bars, clearer labels, less gridline clutter or a purposeful highlight. Write and run **V2**, keeping the original values and the zero baseline, then check both charts again.

```prompt Follow-up starter V2
Keep the independently checked region totals and a zero baseline. [State ONE design improvement.] Regenerate the chart and explain what changed. Do not change the underlying figures or interpret them as profit.
```

### What to submit (as text)

Paste or describe each item; if you include a chart, state its axis, order, labels and whether it was made by the chatbot or by a spreadsheet.

- Your task brief and both prompt versions (V1 and V2).
- The V1 and V2 charts (or screenshots described), each with the true tool or spreadsheet source noted.
- Your four-region verification table, the raw grand-total check and the check method.
- Two or three sentences interpreting the result, and a short revision reflection.
- Tool and model (if visible), run date, CSV filename and any limitations.

### Reflection

1. Could a visually polished chart still be misleading? Give one check that would reveal the problem.
2. Did your design change improve the manager's reading of the comparison? How do you know?
3. What can you conclude about sales differences, and what cannot be inferred from this CSV?
assignments.rubricText:
Practice rubric from the Activity 1 Student sheet: five criteria, each scored 0 (missing or incorrect), 1 (partly met) or 2 (fully met). Total 10 points; the score out of 100 is the total multiplied by 10. Formative unless a course assessor approves a weight.

1. Task and data. 2 points: correct question, exact fields (Store_Region, Net_Sales_Amount) and all four regions.
2. Prompt and run record. 2 points: both prompts (V1, V2) and reproducible execution conditions (tool or model, date, whether the file was really read, fallback disclosed).
3. Independent verification. 2 points: four regional sums and the grand total checked against the source in a spreadsheet, with the check method recorded.
4. Chart integrity. 2 points: correct labels, net sales as the measure, zero baseline, no invented currency.
5. Refinement and interpretation. 2 points: a meaningful V2 change, values and scale rechecked, and an evidence-based statement with no cause, profit or currency claim.

Score 2 only with evidence of the described standard. Alternative defensible outputs (horizontal or vertical bars, different colours, a spreadsheet-made chart) are acceptable: correct numbers, a meaningful design change and transparent provenance matter more than style.

lessons.title: Period 8 · AI-Assisted Prompting
lessons.description: Use AI to draft a prompt plan, then review it and test it fairly. Compare a human-written prompt (A), an AI-drafted workflow (B) and a human-reviewed version (C) on one briefing task with a shared 0/1/2 rubric.
lessons.objectivesLead: By the end of this period you can:
objectives: Explain why AI may help draft a prompt plan and why the draft still needs review and testing
Write a meta-prompt that asks AI to plan and clarify, but not to run the analysis
Review an AI-drafted workflow for invented context, impossible requirements, changed scope and missing checks
Compare a human-written prompt (A), an AI-drafted workflow (B) and a human-reviewed version (C) with one task, one CSV and one five-criterion rubric
State a defensible conclusion when scores differ or tie, and document the versions that led to it
lessons.body:
The regional chart went well, so the manager raises the stakes: *"Next time I want one page, two charts (by region and by product category), three findings I can trust and a note on what the data cannot tell me."* That is a bigger job than Case 1. It involves inspecting the file, calculating two summaries, designing two charts, drawing conclusions and formatting a page. You could write the prompt yourself, or you could ask the chatbot to help you write the prompts. Which is better? You will not decide by how expert the prompt sounds. You will decide by testing the briefings it produces.

> [!ghi-nho] A/B/C compares **prompt-writing methods** on one shared task. It is not a new business case, and its result applies to the runs you actually made, not to every task or model.

:::Predict before you read
Before reading on, write down which of A (you write the prompt), B (AI drafts the prompt plan) and C (you review and edit B) you expect to score highest, and one result that would make you change your mind. At the end of this period you will see what a fair comparison allows you to conclude.
:::

## When AI-assisted prompting helps

Asking AI to draft a prompt plan is useful when:

- the task has **several deliverables** (two charts, three findings, limitations, one page);
- the **process is unclear** and you want AI to suggest stages and ask what is missing;
- the work is **repeated** and you want prompts you can adapt.

What it produces first is a **draft prompt or workflow**, not a verified answer. A generated prompt can change your objective, add assumptions or ask for things you cannot supply. It still needs your review and a test, and length alone is no evidence of quality.

## Define the briefing task and write prompt A

Use one brief for all three approaches.

| Item | Brief |
|---|---|
| Audience | Retail manager |
| Input | The full 200-record retail CSV |
| Deliverables | Two correctly labelled bar charts (net sales by `Store_Region` and by `Product_Category`), three findings backed by checked numbers, an explicit limitations note, one page |
| Success | Figures reconcile to the source, charts are readable and nothing goes beyond the evidence |

```prompt Prompt A — human-written
Using the attached retail transaction CSV, prepare a one-page briefing for a retail manager. Compare summed Net_Sales_Amount by Store_Region and by Product_Category using two bar charts. Include three findings supported by calculations and the main data limitations. Do not invent dates, currency, profit or causal effects.
```

*Assessment:* this may work well, especially in a tool that can analyse files. But it does not say how to check the totals, and it does not say what to do if the interface cannot draw charts. It is a baseline. Whether it is a strong result is something you measure, not assume.

If only verified spreadsheet figures are available, give those figures to the chatbot and ask for a briefing and chart instructions based on them. Do not claim that a file was analysed.

sections.title: 8.3 Ask AI to draft the workflow (B) and review it (C)
sections.intro: Same task, same CSV, three ways of getting to the prompts.

parts.title: A: you write it
parts.md: You write the prompt yourself, without AI drafting help. Save the exact text you run. A is the baseline.

parts.title: B: AI drafts it
parts.md: You give AI the same brief and ask for a plan and prompts, **without running the analysis**. Save the plan exactly as it came back. Do not correct it silently before testing.

parts.title: C: you review B
parts.md: You copy B, mark every edit and improve only what is useful: closing evidence gaps, removing invented or impossible requirements, adding checks.

sections.outro:
Instead of asking for a finished briefing straight away, ask for a plan:

```prompt Meta-prompt B — draft a workflow
Help me turn the one-page retail briefing task into a practical prompt sequence. Ask about any missing requirement that could affect correctness. Then draft prompts for data inspection, summarisation, visualisation and the final briefing. Keep the plan limited to the fields available in the CSV. Do not execute the analysis until I have reviewed the prompts.
```

*Why it is a good meta-prompt:* it asks for clarification before drafting, limits the plan to the fields that exist and separates planning from execution, so you get a chance to review before anything is run.

An **illustrative** reply would propose four stages: (1) inspect rows, columns and valid fields; (2) summarise net sales by region and category; (3) create and check the two charts; (4) write the briefing. This is an instructional outline, not the transcript of a model run. Real replies differ, so read yours with care.

> [!canh-bao] A generated plan can be impressive and still inefficient: pages of output that do not help the manager, a chart tool you do not have, or a quiet assumption that every region has equal store coverage. Ask of each sentence: does it change a requirement I can check?

parts.md:
Review each stage of the AI-drafted plan for the problems below, then add independent verification and clear chart labels before you test.

| Look for | Example in a draft | What you do |
|---|---|---|
| Invented context | A made-up company history, a profit target, a report date | Delete it, or replace it with the manager's real information |
| Impossible requirements | "Show monthly trends" from a file with no dates | Remove the requirement |
| Changed scope | "Compare regions" becomes "rank stores" | Restore the unit you were asked for (the file has no store identifier) |
| Missing checks | No reconciliation of totals | Add a stage that sums each table and compares it with the whole-file total |
| Unavailable tools | An instruction to use a charting tool you do not have | Allow chart specifications as a fallback |
| Redundant text | Pages of persona and tone instructions | Cut anything that does not change a checkable requirement |

The reviewed version keeps the useful stages and closes the gaps. An **illustrative** reviewed sequence:

```prompt Prompt C, stage 1 — inspect
Read the attached CSV. Confirm the number of rows, the column names and what one record represents. Identify the relevant grouping and net-sales fields. State unavailable fields and stop if the file cannot be read.
```

```prompt Prompt C, stage 2 — calculate
Sum Net_Sales_Amount by Store_Region and by Product_Category. Count records. Show the two tables with full-precision totals. Reconcile each table with the same overall net-sales total and explain the aggregation rule. Pause for review.
```

```prompt Prompt C, stages 3–4 — visualise and brief
Use the approved tables to produce two readable, zero-based bar charts (or chart specifications if rendering is unavailable). Label measures and avoid inventing units. Write one page with three evidence-backed findings, data limitations and one question for further investigation. Do not infer causes.
```

*What review added:* a stop if the file cannot be read, a reconciliation step, a pause before charts, a fallback for rendering and a ban on inferring causes. *Human review before use:* confirm that the grouping is by region and category, that the measure is a **sum** of net sales and that nothing is converted into a currency. The two grouped tables must each add up to the same whole-file total, with 200 records.

:::Find the error
An AI-drafted stage reads: "Compare the monthly sales trend of each store, forecast next quarter's profit, and use the best available chart tool to publish the result to the team channel."

How many problems can you find against the brief in section 8.2?
:::

:::Open the solution after you have tried
Four problems. (1) "Monthly" needs dates, which the CSV does not have. (2) "Each store" changes the unit; the file groups by region. (3) "Forecast profit" needs costs and a model of the future, neither of which is in the data or the brief. (4) "Publish to the team channel" gives the draft an action nobody approved; it should stop for human review. Edit C so that none of these survive.
:::

Comparing the prompt texts is not enough. Compare the **briefings** they produce, under matched conditions.

**A fair comparison** keeps these the same for A, B and C: the CSV (or the same verified summary if the tool cannot read files), the brief, the model and tool settings where you can control them, and the output format. Run each variant in a separate clean chat, with its full sequence if it needs several turns. Record the date, tool and any difference that could affect fairness.

Score each final briefing with the course rubric. Each criterion gets 0 (missing or incorrect), 1 (partly met) or 2 (fully met), so a briefing can earn at most **10 points**.

| Criterion | Look for |
|---|---|
| Task | Compares net sales by region and category |
| Figures | Totals match independent checks against the CSV |
| Findings | Three findings follow from the data; limits are stated |
| Coverage | Includes all four regions and every category |
| Presentation | One page, two clear charts and readable labels |

Add time spent and the number of corrections you needed as descriptive effort measures. They help you judge whether a result was worth its cost, but they are not a sixth score.

> [!ghi-nho] No briefing earns full marks for Figures until its region and category totals match your own spreadsheet. Score each criterion separately: accurate numbers cannot make up for missing limitations.

> [!canh-bao] The example scores on the course slide (A = 7, B = 8, C = 9) show how to use the rubric. They are not observed results from a controlled experiment, and they do not show that B or C always wins. A shorter, tested prompt can match a long generated workflow.

sections.title: 8.6 Run and compare A, B and C

parts.md:
1. Record the fixed conditions: CSV filename and version, tool and model, date, output format and any fairness caveat.
2. Write A yourself and save the exact text.
3. Ask AI to draft B (do not run the analysis), then save the plan and prompts exactly as returned.
4. Copy B, mark every edit and write C.
5. Run A, B and C in separate clean chats. Save the three briefings, charts, totals, prompts, settings, time and any failure. Do not invent outputs you did not get.
6. Verify region and category totals independently, then score.
7. Name the version you would reuse for this task, explain why and say what could change the result (another model, a fresh run, another tool).

If a tool cannot read files or draw charts, use **one consistent fallback for all three**: build the tables and charts in a spreadsheet and give the same verified summary to each chatbot run. Say so in your method.

**Reading the result.** If B meets every checked criterion, prefer B unless C shows added value. If A and an AI-drafted prompt tie on the rubric, the defensible statement is "comparable on this task in these runs". Document what you changed: label the AI draft, your edits and the tested result, and keep unsuccessful outputs and their scores. They are part of the evidence.

**Check it yourself.** Build a pivot table with `Store_Region` in rows and SUM of `Net_Sales_Amount` in values, then another with `Product_Category`. Both must add up to 892,252.11 across 200 records.

| **Total** | **200** | **892,252.11** |

The regional totals are in Period 7: North 260,026.33, South 236,980.99, West 213,240.41, East 182,004.38.

**Try it:** (1) explain why comparing final briefings tells you more than comparing prompt lengths; (2) draft prompt A and state two requirements that might be missing; (3) write a meta-prompt for B and name three assumptions you would check in its reply; (4) explain how you would adapt the experiment if only spreadsheet summaries could be analysed.

summary: AI can draft a prompt plan for a complex task. Treat the draft as a proposal to review, never as a validated specification.

questions.prompt: What does AI-assisted prompt generation produce first?
questions.explanation: AI-assisted prompt generation produces a draft prompt or workflow: wording and steps for you to review. It does not produce a verified decision, an audited dataset or a guaranteed better output. The guarantee option is the tempting one because fluent drafts sound authoritative.

options.label: A verified business decision
A draft prompt or workflow
An independently audited dataset
A guaranteed superior output

questions.prompt: What should a learner do with an AI-generated prompt?
questions.explanation: A generated prompt can alter objectives or insert assumptions, so you review its requirements before testing. Publishing it unread, treating it as validated or assuming it contains no invented facts all give the draft more trust than the evidence allows.

options.label: Publish it without reading details
Treat it as a validated specification
Assume it contains no invented facts
Review its requirements before testing

questions.prompt: A one-page briefing needs two charts and three findings. Which requirement should appear explicitly?
questions.explanation: The prompt's output specification should mirror the brief: two charts and three supported findings. A profit forecast is not available in the CSV, a codebase and a paper change the task, and "unlimited charts, optional findings" leaves the deliverables undefined, so they cannot be checked.

options.label: Profit forecasts and margin predictions
A full codebase and a research paper
Two charts and three supported findings
Unlimited charts and optional findings

questions.prompt: An AI drafting assistant asks what decisions the briefing should support. What is the best response?
questions.explanation: When the drafting assistant asks what decisions the briefing should support, give the manager's real decision. That clarifies the objective without fabricating anything. Letting the AI choose, inventing a profit target or replacing the data with a scenario substitutes guesses for facts and distorts the task.

options.label: Ask it to choose any decision
Invent a profit target for context
Replace the data with a scenario
Provide the manager's actual decision

questions.prompt: Why compare variants A, B and C on the same task?
questions.explanation: You compare A, B and C on the same task so that differences in the outputs can be traced to the prompt method, using shared criteria. The comparison is not designed to prove that longer prompts win, to let the third version win or to rank chatbot brands.

options.label: To prove longer prompts are stronger
To make the third version win by design
To assess outputs using shared criteria
To rank chatbot brands by popularity

questions.prompt: AI writes a prompt that requires monthly trends from the undated retail CSV. What should the reviewer change?
questions.explanation: The CSV has no dates, so monthly trends cannot be calculated, and the reviewer must remove that requirement. Keeping it and guessing, relabelling transaction IDs as months or adding a fictional report date all manufacture evidence the file does not contain.

options.label: Keep the request and guess results
Relabel transaction IDs as months
Remove the monthly-trend requirement
Add a fictional report date

questions.prompt: Version C includes more constraints than B, but B meets every checked criterion. What conclusion is warranted?
questions.explanation: Fitness of an output is established by tests, not by prompt length or origin. If B meets every checked criterion, C's extra constraints have shown no value, so prefer B unless C earns a higher score or needs fewer corrections. Scoring C higher for text or complexity rewards length, and discarding B because of where it came from judges origin instead of results.

options.label: Prefer C because it has more text
Score C higher for its complexity
Discard B because AI wrote C
Prefer B unless C shows added value

questions.prompt: In a 0–2 rubric, a briefing has accurate figures but no limitations. Which evaluation is appropriate?
questions.explanation: Rubric criteria are scored separately. Accurate figures earn credit under Figures; the missing limitations cost points under Findings, where limits are expected. Calling the gap a style issue or giving full credit everywhere ignores it, and discarding the accurate figures ignores what the briefing did well.

options.label: Treat the missing caveat as a style issue
Discard accurate figures as unimportant
Give accuracy credit; deduct for limitations
Give full credit on every criterion

questions.prompt: A student asks AI to draft a workflow. Which requested feature makes the draft safer to test?
questions.explanation: Explicit review points between steps give you chances to check assumptions and outputs before the next stage runs, which makes the draft safer to test. A promise that every result is correct, a hidden automatic approval and an instruction to skip source checks all remove control.

options.label: Explicit review points between steps
A promise that every result is correct
A hidden automatic approval stage
An instruction to skip source checks

questions.prompt: An AI-generated prompt silently changes “compare regions” into “rank stores.” What is the primary defect?
questions.explanation: The brief asks to compare regions, and the file does not identify stores. Turning "compare regions" into "rank stores" changes the unit of analysis, so the draft now answers a different question. Brevity, a persona or more examples would not repair that change of scope.

options.label: It makes the wording too concise
It changes the analysis unit
It lacks an elaborate persona
It requests too few examples

questions.prompt: A human-written prompt and an AI-drafted prompt both pass the same rubric. What is the defensible result?
questions.explanation: Equal scores on the same rubric support a narrow, task-specific conclusion: comparable performance in these runs. They do not show that human prompts always win or that AI prompts always win, and a tie is itself a result of testing, not proof that no testing took place.

options.label: Report comparable performance on this task
Claim the human prompt always wins
Assume the tie proves no testing occurred
Claim the AI prompt always wins

questions.prompt: After editing an AI-drafted prompt, how should the learner document it?
questions.explanation: Label the AI draft, your edits and the tested result so the comparison can be audited. Keeping only the final generated text, giving both versions the same name or deleting unsuccessful outputs and scores hides what changed and why.

options.label: Keep only the final generated text
Rename both versions identically
Label the draft, edits and tested result
Delete unsuccessful outputs and scores

questions.explanation: Five criteria at a maximum of 2 points each give 10 points. The slide's example totals (7, 8 and 9) show how to add up the scores; they are not results of a real experiment.

questions.explanation: Fix the conditions before you write anything, write A, get B drafted without running the analysis, derive C from B with marked edits, run all three in clean chats, verify the totals independently and only then score. Scoring before verifying would reward figures you have not checked.
