assignments.title: Activity 2 · Human vs AI-assisted prompt design (A/B/C)
assignments.description:
## Activity 2 · Human vs AI-assisted prompt design (A/B/C)

**Period 8 · about 70 to 90 minutes of practice · CLO2, CLO3, CLO4.** A method comparison on the same retail context; there is no new business case. Full Student sheet: attached to the Module 3 materials lesson.

### One fixed management task

Prepare a one-page retail sales briefing for a manager from the provided CSV. Compare total `Net_Sales_Amount` across all four `Store_Region` values and all four `Product_Category` values. Include **exactly two clear charts** (one by region, one by category), **three findings** backed by checked numbers and the **major data limitations**.

**Controlled comparison.** Keep the data, brief, model or tool, accessible features and output format the same for A, B and C. Compare the briefings each approach produces. Do not reward longer prompts for being longer.

### Files, tools and record

- Source: `Slidescope_Retail_Store_Sales_Enhanced_2025.csv` (200 transactions, 13 columns), an approved chatbot and a spreadsheet. Upload only this permitted CSV.
- If file or chart functions are missing, use **one consistent fallback for all three variants**: build the region and category aggregates and the charts in a spreadsheet and give the same verified summary to each chatbot run. Mark spreadsheet work as such.
- Record before you start: CSV filename and version; tool and model (note if unknown); date, account features and a separate clean chat per variant; output requirement (English, one page, two charts, three findings, limitations); any setting or tool difference that could affect fairness.

### Build the three versions

**A, human-written prompt (10 min).** Write your own complete prompt without asking AI to draft it. Save the exact final text you execute as A.

```prompt A starter brief
Using the retail CSV, prepare a one-page sales briefing comparing total net sales by store region and product category. Include two charts, three findings supported by the data, and the main limitations. [Add the checks and output instructions you think are necessary.]
```

**B, AI-drafted workflow (15 min).** In a preparation chat, give the chatbot the same business brief and the CSV (or the agreed fallback). Answer any clarification with the fixed requirements you recorded. Do not ask it to run the analysis in the drafting conversation.

```prompt Prompt to generate B
Help me turn the fixed one-page retail briefing into an analysis workflow. Ask only important missing questions. Then propose stages and executable prompts for inspecting data, aggregating net sales, making two charts and writing the briefing. Use only the provided CSV; do not do the analysis yet. Preserve the same task, data and required outputs.
```

Save the AI-produced workflow and prompts **exactly** as B. Do not silently correct B before testing. If an instruction asks for private data, invented facts, unsanctioned actions or inaccessible tools, stop, document the issue, obtain an instructor-approved safe substitute and disclose that B was not run unmodified.

**C, human-reviewed B (10 min).** Copy B and mark every edit. Review it for wrong fields, changed scope, omitted categories, hallucinated dates, currency or profit, unclear calculation checks, unachievable chart requirements, risky access and redundant text. Write C by improving only what is useful.

```prompt Review checklist for C
Inspect → Summarise → Visualise → Brief. At each stage, ask what inputs are available, what output must be checked and whether the next stage is safe to proceed. Preserve the brief and the evidence requirements. [Make your own targeted changes to B.]
```

### Execute, evaluate and refine the comparison

1. Open a separate clean run for A, B and C with the same brief, CSV or shared verified inputs, tool or model and output format. If a variant needs several turns, run its full sequence.
2. Save for each variant the final briefing, charts, underlying totals, exact prompts, visible tool settings, time spent and any failures. Do not invent missing outputs.
3. Verify region and category totals independently in the spreadsheet before scoring (PivotTable rows `Store_Region` or `Product_Category`, values SUM of `Net_Sales_Amount`). Confirm that both sets reconcile to the full-file sum.
4. Score the **output** of each variant with the five criteria below, and explain score differences with evidence from the briefings.
5. Choose the approach you would reuse for this task, justify the choice and note what could change the result.

**Verification gate.** No briefing receives full Figures points until its region and category totals match your spreadsheet. If the source cannot be read, describe the fallback and score only what the run actually demonstrated.

### Scorecard (leave blank until you have the outputs)

For every criterion: 2 fully met, 1 partly met, 0 missing or incorrect; maximum 10 per briefing. The slide's example numbers are not a result from your runs.

| Criterion | Look for | A | B | C |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Task | Compares net sales by region and category | | | |
| Figures | Totals match independent checks against the CSV | | | |
| Findings | Three findings follow from the data; limits are stated | | | |
| Coverage | Includes all four regions and every category | | | |
| Presentation | One page, two clear charts and readable labels | | | |
| Total / 10 | Add criterion points | | | |

Also record for each version the final score, total time (minutes) and an execution or fallback note.

### What to submit (as text)

- The exact A prompt, the B prompts as drafted by the AI, and the C prompts with your edits marked.
- Your three briefings, or an accurate description of any failed or incomplete run, with the two-chart requirement checked.
- The region and category verification sheet, the five-criterion scorecard and the effort record.
- A short comparative judgement naming the most useful version in your runs.
- Tool or model, date, file, and stated limits and permissions.

### Reflection

1. Which version met the task with the strongest checked evidence? Point to the output, not prompt length.
2. What did the AI drafter misunderstand or omit? Which C edit addressed a verified weakness?
3. Would another model, a fresh run or a different tool change your result? What would you hold constant?
assignments.rubricText:
Based on the Activity 2 Student sheet. Each criterion is scored 0 (missing or incorrect), 1 (partly met) or 2 (fully met). Total 10 points; the score out of 100 is the total multiplied by 10. Formative unless a course assessor approves a weight.

1. Prompt record. 2 points: the exact A prompt, the B prompts exactly as the AI drafted them, and the C prompts with every edit marked; any case where B could not be run unmodified is disclosed.
2. Fair-comparison record. 2 points: fixed conditions recorded (CSV and version, tool or model, date, a separate clean chat per variant, output format), with a consistent fallback for all three variants if file or chart tools were missing, and any fairness caveat noted.
3. Independent verification. 2 points: region and category totals checked in a spreadsheet, both reconciled to the full-file sum, before any scoring; no full Figures points for a briefing whose totals do not match.
4. Scorecard. 2 points: all five criteria (Task, Figures, Findings, Coverage, Presentation) scored 0, 1 or 2 for each of A, B and C using evidence from the actual briefings, with final scores, time and an execution or fallback note; examples from the slide are not copied.
5. Comparative judgement and reflection. 2 points: names the most useful version in the learner's own runs, points to output evidence rather than prompt length, says what the AI drafter misunderstood or omitted and which C edit fixed a verified weakness, and states what could change the result and what would be held constant.

Do not give credit for invented outputs. If a run was incomplete, score only what was demonstrated.

lessons.title: Period 9 · Reuse and Automate Workflows
lessons.description: Turn the tested briefing into a reusable template, outline a six-stage workflow and an optional skill, and plan scheduled runs with fresh inputs, review gates and failure handling. Know when to keep the work manual.
lessons.objectivesLead: By the end of this period you can:
objectives: Identify repeatable work and distinguish a prompt, template, workflow, skill and automation
Turn a tested briefing prompt into a reusable template with placeholders for file, period and audience
Specify the input, output and check for each of six workflow stages, including what happens when a check fails
Write an automation request that names its source and destination, saves a draft, handles failure and keeps a human review step
Explain why the undated teaching CSV cannot establish a reporting period or support monthly claims
Decide when automation should be deferred and the workflow kept manual
lessons.body:
The manager liked the one-page briefing. *"Can you send me the same thing every month?"* The quickest way is to copy last month's answer and change the title. That is not a report. It is an old answer wearing a new heading. Reuse means keeping a **tested method** and feeding it **fresh data and fresh checks** every time. In this period you turn the Period 8 briefing into a reusable template, think through how to package it as a skill and how to schedule it, and learn when to keep it manual.

> [!ghi-nho] You can reuse the method, the template and the checks. You can never reuse last month's numbers, last month's file or last month's approval.

:::Predict before you read
The CSV you have used is named *Slidescope_Retail_Store_Sales_Enhanced_2025.csv*. Could you start a monthly pipeline by calling it "January"? Write down your answer and what you would need to see in the file or its metadata to justify it. You will check it in section 9.1.
:::

## Spot repeatable work

The Period 8 briefing has a repeatable structure: receive a file, check what it covers, calculate two summaries, make two charts, draft three findings and state the limits. Recurring work with a stable structure is a good candidate for reuse; sensitive, one-off or unsupported tasks are not.

Four words are easy to confuse. They are separate choices, even when a product bundles them in one interface.

| Term | What it is | What it depends on |
|---|---|---|
| **Template** | Reusable prompt text with placeholders such as `[FILE]`, `[REPORTING PERIOD]`, `[AUDIENCE]` | You filling the placeholders each run |
| **Workflow** | Ordered stages with their inputs and review gates | Clear stages and checks |
| **Skill** | A packaged set of instructions and supporting resources, where the product supports it | The product feature and your account |
| **Automation** | A run started by a schedule or trigger | Access to inputs, permissions and tools that really exist |

> [!canh-bao] The slides imagine a future "Month 1" CSV only to explain recurring work. The teaching CSV has **no transaction dates and no month identifier**. It cannot be treated as January, October or any other month. A true month-by-month workflow needs reporting-period metadata, consistent extraction definitions and permission to retrieve each new file.

## Build a reusable template

```prompt Reusable template
Prepare a one-page retail briefing using [APPROVED FILE] for [REPORTING PERIOD] for [AUDIENCE]. Confirm the reporting period is documented in the file or its trusted metadata. Inspect rows and fields. Calculate summed net sales by region and product category and reconcile each table with the whole-file total. Then provide two bar charts or verified chart specifications, three supported findings and limitations. Pause before any distribution or final publication.
```

*Why it works:* the stable parts (task, definitions, chart requirements, checks) stay fixed and the variable parts are placeholders. It asks the model to confirm the reporting period instead of assuming it, includes reconciliation and ends with a pause for a human.

- **Keep:** the task, the metric definitions, the checks and the report layout.
- **Replace each run:** the input file, the reporting period and the audience. A reporting period must come from a trusted source, not from a year in a filename.

Test the template first on an approved input and check that the output really uses the new values. A template that silently keeps old values, or leaves the brackets in the text, is not working.

:::Find the error
Someone saves last month's finished briefing and changes only the title to "March report". Which of the four terms (template, workflow, skill, automation) have they actually used, and what is missing?
:::

:::Open the solution after you have tried
None of them. A saved answer is an output, not a template: it has no placeholders, no stages and no checks, and it contains last month's numbers. The method has not been reused; the result has been recycled.
:::

sections.title: 9.3 Package the workflow as a skill: six stages
sections.intro: Where the product supports it, a skill packages a tested set of instructions and resources (the template, the metric definitions, the checks). Keep the method simple enough to run as ordinary saved prompts when skills are unavailable. For each stage, define who supplies the input, what is produced and what can stop progress.

parts.title: 1. Receive
parts.md:
**Input:** approved CSV and a documented reporting period.

**Output:** an identified file version.

**Check:** correct permission and scope.

parts.title: 2. Inspect
parts.md:
**Input:** the original file.

**Output:** a row and field inventory.

**Check:** expected columns are present; transaction IDs are unique.

parts.title: 3. Calculate
parts.md:
**Input:** checked records.

**Output:** the two grouping tables.

**Check:** sums and counts reconcile to the whole file.

parts.title: 4. Visualise
parts.md:
**Input:** verified tables.

**Output:** two charts or specifications.

**Check:** axes, categories, totals and readable labels.

parts.title: 5. Draft
parts.md:
**Input:** verified evidence.

**Output:** a one-page briefing.

**Check:** findings are qualified and unknowns are disclosed.

parts.title: 6. Approve
parts.md:
**Input:** the reviewed document.

**Output:** an approved distribution copy.

**Check:** the manager approves external use.

sections.outro:
**A failed check produces an exception report, not a polished briefing.** If `Net_Sales_Amount` is missing, calculation stops and the workflow asks for a valid extract. It does not invent the column or fall back to old data. Test that your skill asks for missing inputs rather than quietly reusing earlier ones.

> [!meo] What belongs in a skill: input requirements, metric definitions, the report template and the verification steps. What does not: passwords, access tokens, broad posting permissions or promises of accuracy.

parts.md:
A skill stores the method. An automation runs it. Scheduling works only when the account has the right tool, permissions, access to the input and a tested run plan. A text document or a folder of saved prompts is a fully valid alternative for learners without these features.

If scheduling is available, an **illustrative** automation request might read:

```prompt Automation specification — do not run without approval
On an approved monthly schedule, obtain the previous reporting period's permitted extract from [APPROVED SOURCE]. Run the tested briefing workflow. Save a draft in [APPROVED DESTINATION], record the file version and calculations, and notify the reviewer. Never send a management report or modify source data without explicit human approval. If the file is missing or its columns have changed, flag the failure.
```

*Why it is safer than "send me the report every month":* it names the source and destination, saves a **draft** rather than sending, records the file version and calculations, says what to do on failure and keeps a human in charge of distribution.

A scheduling instruction alone cannot grant file access, define a data pipeline or establish compliance. Before you automate, confirm who owns the input, what the destination permissions are, what the retention rules say and who is responsible for review. If you cannot establish those, **keep the manual version** and still keep the method documentation. Test one manual run before you schedule anything.

Test the next run with an approved replacement file or a changed brief. Check that it recalculates the results, reports missing columns clearly and asks for human review before publication.

**An illustrative test.** Copy the checked CSV to a separate learning folder and name it so its role is obvious. Supply it through the template and verify that the output still reconciles to 892,252.11 across 200 records. This tests a known reference file. It is not proof of a real monthly pipeline.

**For a genuine second extract,** compare the field definitions, the transaction coverage, the unique IDs and the grouping totals before you use it. A difference in total sales may reflect a change in the source's scope as well as in business activity.

| If the new file... | The workflow should... |
|---|---|
| Lacks the net-sales column | Stop at inspection and report the missing column; do not invent or substitute one |
| Has only three regions | Report the missing region and ask whether the extract is incomplete before any chart |
| Has different field definitions | Flag the difference and retest before reuse |
| Has no documented period | Ask for the period; do not infer it from a filename |

**Try it:** (1) name three placeholders you need to reuse the briefing next month; (2) explain why the uploaded CSV cannot establish its own reporting period; (3) make a one-page checklist with one check per stage; (4) give one reason to keep the workflow manual until access and approval are confirmed.

items.meaning: Reusable instructions with replaceable inputs. The stable parts stay fixed; the file, period and audience change each run.
items.example: Prepare a briefing using [FILE] for [PERIOD] for [AUDIENCE].

items.meaning: Ordered stages with their inputs, outputs and review gates: receive, inspect, calculate, visualise, draft, approve.
Platform-dependent packaging of instructions and resources (template, metric definitions, checks). Not available in every tool; saved prompts are a valid fallback.
A run started by a schedule or trigger. It can use only the inputs, permissions and tools that actually exist.
A point where a person validates or approves an output before work continues or anything is distributed.
The time span a file covers. It must come from trusted metadata, not from a filename or a guess.
items.note: The teaching CSV has no dates, so it cannot be "January".

items.meaning: What the workflow produces when a check fails: a clear description of the problem, not a polished briefing.
Every run recalculates from the new input and repeats the checks. An old answer with a new title is not a report.
A versioned template, the input file version and a log of checks together, so another person can repeat the run.
Stay manual until input ownership, destination permissions, retention rules and review responsibility are confirmed.

summary: Reuse a tested method, never an old answer: a template has placeholders, a workflow has stages and review gates, a skill packages them where supported, and an automation runs them on a trigger.
Each run needs fresh data, a trusted reporting period and fresh checks. The teaching CSV has no dates, so it cannot stand in for a month.
When a check fails the workflow produces an exception report, and a person approves anything that leaves the team.
Optional tools may package or schedule the work. Their availability does not remove the need for permission, verification and human approval, and a manual workflow is a valid choice.

questions.prompt: Which task is a strong candidate for prompt reuse?
questions.explanation: Prompt reuse suits recurring work with a stable structure, such as a weekly sales briefing. A password request is sensitive and one-off, a unique apology is not repeatable and an undocumented guess about demand is not worth preserving. The one-off options are tempting because they feel important, but nothing in them recurs.

options.label: A private one-time password request
A recurring weekly sales briefing
A unique unrepeatable apology
An undocumented guess about demand

questions.prompt: A reusable prompt uses [FILE] and [AUDIENCE]. What should happen each run?
questions.explanation: A reusable template separates stable instructions from variable inputs, so each run replaces placeholders with the current file, period and audience. Hardcoding the first file, leaving placeholders in the output or assuming last month's values persist makes the result stale or incomplete.

options.label: Hardcode the first file permanently
Replace placeholders with current inputs
Leave the placeholders in the output
Assume last month's values persist

questions.prompt: In the course, a skill mainly packages what?
questions.explanation: In this course a skill packages reusable instructions and supporting resources, such as the template, the metric definitions and the checks. It does not create a new data model, guarantee approval or fix financial facts like a currency rate.

options.label: A new proprietary data model
A guaranteed autonomous approval
A fixed monthly currency rate
Reusable instructions and resources

questions.prompt: A scheduled report relies on a monthly file that might be missing. What should the workflow specify?
questions.explanation: The workflow should check that the source file exists before it calculates, and stop with a clear exception if it does not. Omitting the date, reusing older numbers silently or inventing a file would deliver a stale or false report. Being scheduled on time does not make the data current.

options.label: Omit the report date without explanation
Reuse the older numbers without notice
Invent a source file if missing
Check that the source file exists

questions.prompt: A class has no access to scheduled tasks. How can it practise workflow design?
questions.explanation: Without scheduling tools you can still practise workflow design: a manual run checklist teaches the same planning and verification. Do not remove human approval, assume everyone has the feature or claim that an automatic run took place. A feature you did not use cannot be reported as used.

options.label: Remove all human approval steps
Create and test a manual run checklist
Assume every student has the feature
Claim an automatic run took place

questions.prompt: What remains necessary for scheduled AI drafts?
questions.explanation: Scheduled creation of a draft is not distribution: a person reviews the draft before it is sent. Hidden replacement of source data, unrestricted folder access and permanent permission to publish give automation more authority than it should have.

options.label: Hidden replacement of source data
Unrestricted access to all folders
Human review before distribution
Permanent permission to publish

questions.prompt: A monthly template uses a new CSV without dates. What is the most serious risk?
questions.explanation: Monthly claims require dated records and documented coverage, and this CSV has neither, so calling its totals a monthly trend is the serious risk. A consistent table format, an audience line and a renamed placeholder are harmless when the content is checked.

options.label: Calling the result a monthly trend
Keeping a consistent table format
Listing the target audience
Renaming the input placeholder

questions.prompt: A student packages a briefing workflow as a skill. What should be included?
questions.explanation: A skill should carry what makes reuse safe: input requirements and verification steps. Unrestricted posting permissions, claims of guaranteed accuracy and private login details are unnecessary in a packaged workflow and make it riskier.

options.label: Input requirements and verification steps
Unrestricted posting permissions
Claims of guaranteed model accuracy
Private login tokens and passwords

questions.prompt: A template worked once, then the reporting file structure changed. What is the right next step?
questions.explanation: A changed file structure can break calculations or change what a column means, so you retest the workflow with the new columns before reuse. Assuming the old instructions fit, using the previous output as new data or hiding the field changes lets the break pass unnoticed.

options.label: Use the previous output as new data
Assume the old instructions still fit
Retest the workflow with new columns
Hide the field changes in the report

questions.prompt: A team wants reproducible weekly summaries. Which setup is strongest?
questions.explanation: Reproducing weekly summaries needs the instructions (a versioned template), the input (a specific file version) and evidence of verification (a check log). A chart without its data, a promise to remember or unlabelled screenshots cannot be re-run or audited.

options.label: Versioned template, input file and check log
Saved chart image without input data
A promise to remember last week's work
Unlabeled screenshots of successive chats

questions.prompt: Match each term to its description.
questions.explanation: A template is reusable text with placeholders, a workflow is ordered stages with review gates, a skill is packaged instructions and resources where a product supports it, and an automation is a scheduled or triggered run limited by access. A review gate is the point where a person checks or approves.

pairs.right: Ordered stages with inputs and review gates
Packaged instructions and resources, where the product supports it
A scheduled or triggered run, limited by the access it has
A point where a person checks or approves before work continues

questions.prompt: A year in a CSV's filename is a reliable way to establish the file's reporting period for a monthly report.
questions.explanation: False. A reporting period should come from the data (a date or period field) or trusted metadata. A filename is a label anyone can change, and a year alone cannot identify a month or confirm what the file covers.

options.label: True
False

questions.prompt: Put the six stages of the briefing workflow in order.
questions.explanation: The workflow starts with an approved, identified input, inspects it, calculates and reconciles before any chart, builds charts from verified tables, drafts from verified evidence and ends with human approval. Drafting before reconciling would write findings on unchecked figures.
sequence: Receive an approved input with a documented reporting period
Inspect the data: rows, fields, duplicate IDs
Calculate and reconcile the two grouping tables
Create the charts from verified tables
Draft the one-page summary with limitations

misconceptions.name: Mixes up the order of the five-step cycle
misconceptions.description: You treat the stages as interchangeable, for example redefining the objective or rewriting constraints right after the tool answers. Each stage uses the output of the one before, and the first check against the source belongs before anything is published or refined. Sign: you jump from "the tool answered" straight to another action.

misconceptions.name: Reads or asks for more than the CSV can support
misconceptions.description: You infer profit, demand, efficiency, growth or causes from totals of net sales, or you ask for forecasts, visits or monthly figures the file does not contain. The CSV has regions, categories and sales amounts for 200 undated transactions, nothing more. Sign: your claim needs a column you cannot point to.

misconceptions.name: Accepts a scale that distorts bar lengths
misconceptions.description: You think the axis is a free design choice: truncating it, hiding its labels or scaling each bar separately seems harmless. Bars encode value by length, so only a shared zero baseline keeps lengths proportional to values. Sign: small differences look large, or readers cannot tell what the axis shows.

misconceptions.name: Accepts a chart or prompt because it looks polished
misconceptions.description: You treat appearance (colours, fonts, animation, a striking look) as a sign that the numbers and claims are right. Looks tell you nothing about whether the measure, totals, labels and statements are correct. Sign: you praise the design before recalculating anything.

misconceptions.name: Assumes the tool did something it did not do
misconceptions.description: You write as if every chatbot can open files and draw charts, or you accept coordinates, descriptions or an "unseen chart" as if they had been produced. A capability counts only when you can see the output and its source. Sign: you cannot say how the chart was made.

misconceptions.name: Treats one problem as proof that everything is right or wrong
misconceptions.description: You react to a single issue by deleting everything, doubting every number, or you accept everything because one part is correct. Totals, chart and narrative can be judged separately: keep what passes its check and repair what fails. Sign: your fix is "start over" or "publish as is".

misconceptions.name: Discards the prompts, outputs and checks
misconceptions.description: You keep only the final picture, or you rename or delete earlier versions once the chart is finished. Without both prompts, both outputs and the check results nobody, including you, can see what changed or reproduce the totals. Sign: you cannot show what V1 looked like.

misconceptions.name: Trusts an AI-drafted prompt or plan without reviewing it
misconceptions.description: You treat a generated prompt as a finished, validated specification, publish it unread or remove the human checks from the workflow. A draft can change your objective, add invented facts or skip verification, and nothing in it guarantees a better result. Sign: you test or run the plan without reading it first.

misconceptions.name: Treats a longer or more elaborate prompt as a better prompt
misconceptions.description: You assume more text, more constraints, a persona or a more complex workflow means a stronger result, or you try to fix a problem by adding words. Quality is shown by what the tested output achieves against the criteria, not by how the prompt sounds. Sign: you prefer a version because it is longer or more complex.

misconceptions.name: Misreads what a fair prompt comparison is for
misconceptions.description: You treat the comparison as a way to make a favoured version win, to rank products or to prove a universal rule such as "AI always wins". A fair comparison holds task, data and criteria constant so you can say what happened in these runs. Sign: your conclusion is wider than your evidence, or the design favours one version.

misconceptions.name: Fills gaps in the task with invented facts
misconceptions.description: When a requirement cannot be met from the file or brief, you supply a guess: a target, a report date, a scenario in place of the data, or you relabel columns. Invented context makes the output look complete while quietly changing the task. Sign: the briefing mentions something nobody told the AI.

misconceptions.name: Lets the task specification drift from the brief
misconceptions.description: You accept or write requirements that differ from the brief: extra deliverables, forecasts the file cannot support, optional outputs, or a changed unit of analysis. The prompt should mirror the brief so the result can be checked against it. Sign: the output list or the grouping no longer matches what the manager asked for.

misconceptions.name: Blends rubric criteria instead of scoring each separately
misconceptions.description: You let one strong criterion lift or sink the others: accurate figures excuse missing limitations, or a missing caveat is waved away as style. Each criterion measures something different and is scored on its own evidence. Sign: your scores for all criteria rise and fall together.

misconceptions.name: Does not keep a labelled trail of versions and results
misconceptions.description: You keep only the final text, give versions the same name or delete weak outputs and scores once you have a winner. Without the draft, your edits and the tested results, nobody can tell what changed or whether the comparison was fair. Sign: you cannot say which edit improved which weakness.

misconceptions.name: Picks one-off, sensitive or unsupported tasks for reuse
misconceptions.description: You choose tasks to save as templates because they feel important, not because they repeat. Reuse pays off when work recurs with a stable structure. A one-time sensitive request, a unique message or an undocumented guess has nothing to template. Sign: the task cannot be described by fixed steps and replaceable inputs.

misconceptions.name: Reuses old inputs, outputs or unresolved placeholders
misconceptions.description: You treat reuse as copying: keeping the first file, last month's values, an earlier output as new data, or leaving brackets in the text. A reusable template separates stable instructions from variable inputs and fills every placeholder from the current run. Sign: this run's report contains something from the last one.

misconceptions.name: Fills a missing or changed input without telling anyone
misconceptions.description: When a source file is missing or its structure changes you carry on anyway: omitting the date, reusing older numbers, inventing a source or hiding the change. The result looks complete but rests on something false or stale. Sign: nobody is told that an input is missing or different.

misconceptions.name: Credits a skill or schedule with powers it does not have
misconceptions.description: You expect a skill or automation to supply new data, approve reports, fix facts such as exchange rates or guarantee accuracy, or you assume or pretend that a feature exists. They only run what you have defined, with the access you have actually set up. Sign: you cannot say where the input comes from or who approves the result.

misconceptions.name: Gives automation access, credentials or authority it should not have
misconceptions.description: You remove human approval, grant broad folder access, allow permanent publishing rights or put passwords and tokens inside a packaged workflow. Automation drafts; people approve and distribute. Sign: nobody reviews before something leaves the team, or the workflow holds secrets.

misconceptions.name: Assumes a reporting period without trusted metadata
misconceptions.description: You treat an undated file as if it supported month-by-month statements, taking the period from a filename, a year or an assumption. Monthly claims need dated records and documented coverage. Sign: your report says "monthly" or "trend" but you cannot point to a date field or period metadata.

misconceptions.name: Keeps too little to reproduce the run
misconceptions.description: You rely on a chart image, a screenshot, a promise to remember or a set of unlabelled chats. Reproducing a result needs the instructions, the input version and the checks that were made. Sign: another person could not repeat your run.

feedbackTemplates.body: Write down what each of the five stages produces and what the next stage needs from it. Then find the point where you first compare the tool's output with the CSV. Anything you publish, refine or redefine before that point rests on an unchecked output.

For each claim or request, name the column in the CSV that would support it. If you cannot, the claim or the request goes beyond the data. A ranking of sums supports a statement about recorded net sales and nothing about profit, demand, efficiency or causes.

Look at the first tick on the value axis. If it is not zero, bar lengths no longer match values; a bar for 70% of the maximum can look tiny. A fair chart for comparing sizes uses one shared zero baseline with labelled units. Hiding the labels hides the problem; it does not fix it.

Set the visuals aside and check three things: do the labels name the right measure, do the totals match your own spreadsheet, and is every sentence supported by a number? A good-looking chart can be wrong and a plain one can be right. Decide on the checks, then on the design.

Ask what evidence shows that the tool read the file and drew the chart: a row count, a table you can recompute, a visible image. If the tool cannot do it, use a spreadsheet or request a specification you can build elsewhere, and state which part came from where.

Split the output into parts (totals, labels, scale, order, commentary) and check each one. Keep the parts that pass, fix the ones that fail, and recheck after the change. Throwing away verified work wastes effort, and publishing unsupported text because the chart is right passes a claim you never tested.

Save every prompt version with its output, the tool and date, the input filename and the checks you made. Label versions honestly and never rename an early draft as final. A peer should be able to repeat your totals from the record without using the AI output.

Read the draft requirement by requirement and compare it with your brief: does each line keep the objective, use only fields in the CSV and leave a place for you to check before the next stage? A draft is a proposal. What makes a plan safe to test is the review points you keep or add, not the confidence of its wording.

Ask what each extra sentence changes that you can check. Then compare the outputs, not the prompts: if a shorter version meets every criterion, the extra length has not earned anything. Match the fix to the defect; a wrong unit or scope is not repaired by more detail.

Write the conclusion you are entitled to: which version did what, on this task, under these conditions. Check that everything except the prompt method was held constant, and that no version was favoured by sequence, effort or origin. A tie supports a statement about this task and nothing broader.

Ask what the file or the manager actually supplies for this requirement. If the answer is nothing, either ask the manager for the real information or remove the requirement. Never fill the gap with a guess; mark it as unknown and state it in the limitations.

Put the brief and the prompt side by side and tick off the outputs, the grouping unit and the data used. Anything in the prompt that is not in the brief, or in the file, is drift; anything missing from the prompt is a gap. A precise brief states exactly what must be produced.

Score one criterion at a time, pointing to the part of the briefing that is your evidence. Accurate numbers earn credit where numbers are scored; a gap elsewhere costs points where that is scored. If you cannot point to evidence for a 2, it is not a 2.

Label each version (A, B as drafted, C with edits marked) and keep its output, settings, time and score together. Keep the unsuccessful runs, since they show what the edits fixed. A reviewer should be able to follow the trail from the first draft to the final briefing.

Ask whether the task recurs, whether its steps stay the same and which parts change each time. Recurring work with a stable structure and variable inputs is a template candidate. Sensitive, unrepeatable or unsupported items are not, and putting them into a saved prompt spreads the problem.

Before each run, list the placeholders and write the current value for each. Check that no earlier file, number or output feeds the new run, and that no bracket is left in the result. If the file structure changed, retest before you reuse the instructions.

Make the workflow check that the source exists and has the expected columns before it calculates. If a check fails, produce an exception report that says what is missing or changed and stop. Never replace the missing item with an invented or older one without saying so.

Write down what the feature really does: which instructions and resources it holds, which inputs it needs and which permissions it has. Anything beyond that is your responsibility. If you do not have the feature, practise with a manual checklist and say so honestly.

Give the workflow the least access it needs: a named source, a named destination and draft-only output. Keep credentials out of saved instructions, and keep a review gate before any distribution or publication.

Check the file for a date or period field and for documentation from a trusted source. If neither exists, do not claim a period or trend; ask for period-labelled data. Formatting, audience lines and placeholder names are not the risk here: unsupported time claims are.

List what a stranger would need to rerun your work: the versioned template, the exact input file and the log of checks. Anything that is only in your memory or in an unlabelled screenshot cannot be audited, so save it with a label.
